entry: Northern constituent country of the [[United Kingdom]] (pop., 2022: 5,436,600). It occupies the northern part of the island of Great Britain and adjacent islands. Its capital is [[Edinburgh]], and Glasgow is the largest city. Scotland borders England to the south, with the Atlantic Ocean to the north and west and the North Sea to the east. The Highlands contain [[Ben Nevis]], at 4,413 feet (1,345 m) the highest peak in the British Isles. The Kingdom of Scotland emerged as a sovereign state in the 9th century and remained independent until 1707, when it united with England to form the [[Kingdom of Great Britain]]. A Scottish Parliament was re-established in 1999 and holds authority over many domestic policies. [[Scottish Gaelic]] is largely spoken in the Hebrides, and its speakers make up less than 2% of the population.

West Germanic language descended from Early Middle English and closely related to [[Modern English]]. It is an official language of [[Scotland]] and is listed by [[UNESCO]] as a vulnerable language. In the 2022 census, 1,508,540 people in Scotland aged three and over reported being able to speak Scots. It is spoken mainly in the Lowlands, the Northern Isles and northern [[Ulster]]. Scholars disagree whether Scots is a dialect of [[English language|English]] or a separate language.

American composer and pianist, dubbed the "King of Ragtime." He composed more than 40 ragtime pieces, one ragtime ballet and two operas. His "Maple Leaf Rag" (1899) became the genre's first and most influential hit, selling nearly 500,000 copies over the following decade. Joplin considered [[Ragtime|ragtime]] a form of [[Classical music|classical music]] meant for concert halls. He moved to Sedalia, [[Missouri]], in 1894 and later to St. Louis and New York City. In 1916 he descended into dementia from [[Syphilis|neurosyphilis]]. His music revived in the early 1970s, helped by the Academy Award–winning film *The Sting* (1973), and in 1976 he was posthumously awarded a [[Pulitzer Prize]] for his opera *Treemonisha*.

Celtic language native to the Gaels of [[Scotland]], developed from Old Irish and related to [[Irish language|Irish]] and Manx. It became a distinct spoken language in the 13th century. The 2022 census recorded 130,161 people with some skills in Gaelic, of whom 69,701 reported speaking it. A dialect known as Canadian Gaelic has been spoken in [[Canada]] since the 18th century, with a concentration of speakers in [[Nova Scotia]]. The Scottish Languages Act 2025 made Gaelic, alongside [[Scots language|Scots]], an official language of Scotland.

Historical region of northern [[Scotland]] containing [[Ben Nevis]], the highest mountain in the [[British Isles]]. Its [[Scottish Gaelic]] name, a' Ghàidhealtachd, means "the place of the Gaels." The population density of the Highlands and Islands was 9.1 per sq km (24 per sq mi) in 2012. Emigration exceeded natural population increase for about 160 years from c. 1841. The region has the only boreal forest biome in the British Isles, with concentrated populations of Scots pine.

Youth movement popularly established in the first decade of the 20th century, following the Scout method of informal education through outdoor activities such as [[Camping|camping]], woodcraft, aquatics, [[Hiking|hiking]] and sports. A widely recognized characteristic is the Scout [[Uniform|uniform]], which by intent hides differences of social standing and encourages equality. Distinctive insignia include the [[Fleur-de-lis]] and merit badges. Girls-only organizations, whose members are often called Guides, use a trefoil instead. The original program was for youths aged 11 to 17, and younger and older programs also exist. In 2019, over 55 million Scouts and Guides were in at least 155 countries. Robert Baden-Powell tested his ideas at an experimental camp on Brownsea Island in 1907 and published *Scouting for Boys* in 1908.

Crossword-style [[Board game|board game]] for two to four players, who score points by placing letter tiles on a 15×15 grid to form words listed in a standard [[Dictionary|dictionary]]. American architect Alfred Mosher Butts invented it in 1931 as Criss-Crosswords. James Brunot bought the manufacturing rights in 1948, renamed the game Scrabble and licensed it to Selchow and Righter in 1952. About 150 million sets have been sold worldwide, and there are approximately 4,000 Scrabble clubs around the world. An English-language set contains 100 tiles, 98 of them lettered with point values from 1 to 10. Hasbro produces the game in the United States and Canada, and Mattel manufactures it elsewhere.

Externally threaded [[Fastener|fastener]] tightened or loosened by torque applied to its head. Most screws hold objects together, and the head usually has a slot or other feature that takes a tool such as a screwdriver. Most screws have a right-hand thread. Left-hand threads are used where counterclockwise torque would loosen a right-hand screw, as on the left pedal of a bicycle. The screw first appeared in Mesopotamia during the Neo-Assyrian period (911–609 BC), and Archytas of Tarentum (428–350 BC) described it in Greece. Metal screws were rare in Europe before the 15th century and became common only after machine tools for mass production developed toward the end of the 18th century. The [[Screw mechanism|screw mechanism]] is one of the six classical simple machines defined by Renaissance scientists.

Mechanism that converts rotational motion and torque into linear motion and force, one of the six classical [[Simple machine|simple machines]]. Geometrically, a screw is a narrow [[Inclined plane|inclined plane]] wrapped around a cylinder. A smaller pitch gives greater mechanical advantage. Screw mechanisms are used in threaded [[Fastener|fasteners]], screw jacks, vises and screw presses. The [[Archimedes' screw|Archimedes' screw]] is a water pump with a rotating helical chamber. The water screw was first used in [[Ancient Egypt]], before [[Archimedes]] described his pump around 234 BC. In 1600, [[Galileo Galilei]] worked out the complete dynamic theory of simple machines in *Le Meccaniche* ("On Mechanics").

Roll of [[Papyrus|papyrus]], [[Parchment|parchment]] or [[Paper|paper]] containing writing, also called a roll. Scrolls were the first form of editable record keeping, used in [[Ancient Egypt]]. Text was written in lines from top to bottom, and the scroll was unrolled one page at a time. Parchment scrolls were used by the [[Israelites]] before the [[Codex|codex]], a folded bound book, became popular around the 1st century AD. Scrolls were more highly regarded than codices until well into Roman times. A Chinese "whirlwind book" consisted of several sheets of paper bound at the top with [[Bamboo|bamboo]] and rolled up. A legend credits [[Julius Caesar]] with folding scrolls into codex form, but the surviving passage is unclear.

External male genitalia of most terrestrial [[Mammal|mammals]], a sac of skin at the base of the [[Penis|penis]]. It contains the [[Testicle|testicles]], epididymides and vasa deferentia, and usually tightens in cold temperatures. The scrotum regulates the temperature of the testicles and maintains it at 35 °C (95 °F). [[Testosterone]] masculinizes the labioscrotal folds into the scrotum during development. At [[Puberty|puberty]], it darkens the scrotal skin and promotes [[Pubic hair|pubic hair]]. The scrotum is homologous to the labia majora in females.

Racing division of the Italian automaker [[Ferrari]] and its [[Formula One]] team, known as the "Prancing Horse." Founded by [[Enzo Ferrari]] in 1929 to race Alfa Romeo cars, it is the oldest surviving Formula One team and has competed in every World Championship since 1950. It holds the records for 16 Constructors' Championships and 15 Drivers' Championships, the latter won by nine drivers. [[Michael Schumacher]] won five consecutive drivers' titles from 2000 to 2004. The Italian Grand Prix at Monza is regarded as the team's home race.

Deficiency disease caused by a lack of [[Vitamin C]] (ascorbic acid). Early symptoms include weakness, fatigue and sore arms and legs. Untreated, it can cause gum disease, decreased red blood cells and poor [[Wound|wound]] healing. It takes at least a month of little or no vitamin C in the diet before symptoms appear. Humans and a few other species cannot make their own vitamin C. Historically, scurvy killed large numbers of sailors on long sea voyages. In 1747, Scottish physician James Lind showed that citrus fruits could treat it. Treatment is with vitamin C supplements, taken by mouth or given intravenously.

Fast-moving [[Centipede|centipede]] species, also known as the house centipede. It is typically yellowish-gray and has up to 15 pairs of long legs. Originating in the Mediterranean region, it has spread to many parts of the world and often lives in and around human homes. It preys on [[Insect|insects]] and [[Spider|spiders]] by envenomating them, and its mild [[Venom|venom]] and small organs of envenomation make it nearly incapable of harming humans. [[Carl Linnaeus]] described it in 1758 as *Scolopendra coleoptrata*, and [[Jean-Baptiste Lamarck]] placed it in the genus *Scutigera* in 1801.

Ancient Eastern Iranic [[Nomad|nomadic]] equestrian people of the Pontic Steppe, in modern [[Ukraine]] and southern [[Russia]]. They migrated there from Central Asia in the 9th to 8th centuries BC and displaced the Agathyrsi and Cimmerians as the dominant power on the western Eurasian steppe. In the 7th century BC they crossed the [[Caucasus Mountains]] and raided [[West Asia]], until the Medes expelled them in the 6th century BC. Later conquered by the [[Sarmatians]] in the 3rd to 2nd centuries BC, the Scythians were absorbed by successive populations in the early [[Middle Ages]]. Later writers applied the name Scythians to many unrelated steppe peoples.

Marketing name for brine shrimp (*Artemia*) sold as novelty aquarium pets. Harold von Braunhut developed the product in the United States in 1957 and sold it under the Sea-Monkeys name from 1962. The eggs are most often sold in a kit of three pouches, and the product was heavily advertised in [[Comic book|comic books]] in the 1960s and 1970s. Under ideal home conditions the animals may live up to five years, although they usually live two to three months. Because they are easy to breed, brine shrimp are also widely used as a [[Model organism|model organism]] in research on developmental biology, [[Genetics|genetics]] and [[Toxicology|toxicology]].

Group of tribes that raided [[Egypt]] and other eastern Mediterranean regions around 1200 BC, during the [[Bronze Age]]. The term "Sea Peoples" is a modern coinage and is often considered a misnomer, because most of the groups appear to have traveled by land. The concept originated with 19th-century Egyptologists Emmanuel de Rougé, curator of the [[Louvre]], and Gaston Maspero, who drew on reliefs at the temple of [[Ramesses III]] at Medinet Habu. Early scholars often regarded them as a primary cause of the Bronze Age Collapse, but more recent scholarship views them as refugees fleeing a crisis already under way.

Predatory marine [[Invertebrate|invertebrate]] of the order Actiniaria, related to [[Coral|corals]] and [[Jellyfish|jellyfish]] in the phylum [[Cnidaria]]. A typical sea anemone is a single polyp with a column topped by an oral disc, a ring of tentacles and a central [[Mouth|mouth]]. Its tentacles carry stinging cells and can be retracted or extended to catch prey. Many species host symbiotic dinoflagellates or algae, and some live alongside [[Clownfish|clownfish]]. Sea anemones release sperm and eggs through the mouth, and the larvae settle to develop into juvenile polyps. They can also reproduce asexually by breaking into pieces that regenerate.

Class of [[Echinoderm|echinoderms]] (Holothuroidea) found on the sea floor worldwide, with about 1,786 known species, most in the Asia–Pacific region. Sea cucumbers are detritivores that break down organic matter and help recycle nutrients in the marine ecosystem. They have leathery skin and an elongated body, and are named for their resemblance to the fruit of the [[Cucumber|cucumber]] plant. Their calcified skeleton is usually reduced to microscopic ossicles joined by [[Connective tissue|connective tissue]]. Many species are harvested as food, and some are cultivated in [[Aquaculture|aquaculture]] systems. They are considered a delicacy in Asian cuisines, where they are called trepang, namako or bêche-de-mer.

Frozen seawater that floats on the ocean's surface, distinct from [[Iceberg|icebergs]], which are chunks of ice shelves or glaciers. Sea ice covers about 7% of the Earth's surface and about 12% of the world's oceans, much of it in the polar ice packs of the [[Arctic Ocean]] and the [[Southern Ocean]]. Brine channels within the ice support [[Microorganism|microorganisms]] that form the base of food webs. Its white surface reflects sunlight back into space, a process known as the [[Albedo|albedo]] effect, and it limits the exchange of heat and [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] between the sea and the atmosphere. Satellite records show a marked decline in Arctic sea ice extent and thickness, a trend linked to [[Climate change|climate change]].

Average surface level of Earth's coastal waters, used as a [[Geodetic datum|vertical datum]] for measuring heights. Mean sea level is the chart datum for [[Cartography|cartography]] and marine [[Navigation|navigation]], and in aviation it is the standard against which altitude is calibrated. A common standard is a long-term average of tide gauge readings at a given site, since the sea is affected by [[Tide|tides]], [[Wind|wind]] and air pressure. The [[Geoid|geoid]] dips as much as 106 m (348 ft) below global mean sea level in the Indian Ocean. A finding from 2026 holds that sea levels estimated with the geoid used in 90% of published work were about 25 cm lower than measured values on average, underestimating the effect of sea level rise.

[[Pinniped|Pinniped]] with external ear flaps, long foreflippers and the ability to walk on all fours. Sea lions form the family Otariidae with the fur seals, collectively known as [[Eared seal|eared seals]]. There are six extant species in five [[Genus|genera]], ranging from subarctic to tropical waters in both hemispheres, except the northern [[Atlantic Ocean]]. Sea lions live 20–30 years. The largest, the Steller sea lion, can weigh 1,000 kg (2,200 lb) and reach a length of 3.0 m (10 ft). Three species, the Australian, Galápagos and New Zealand sea lions, are endangered.

Shallow inland shelf sea in Eastern Europe, connected to the [[Black Sea]] by the Strait of Kerch. It is bounded by [[Russia]] to the east and [[Ukraine]] to the northwest and southwest, and Ukrainian parts of the coast have been under Russian occupation since 2022. The sea is the shallowest in the world, with depths between 0.9 and 14 meters (3 and 46 ft). Inflow from the [[Don (river)|Don]] and Kuban rivers keeps its water low in salinity and rich in plankton, supporting high fish productivity. Water constantly flows out of the sea into the Black Sea. The sea is an access route from the [[Caspian Sea]] via the Volga–Don Canal. In antiquity it was known as the Maeotis Swamp, and [[Herodotus]] judged it as large as the Black Sea.

Marginal sea between the Japanese archipelago, [[Sakhalin]], the [[Korea|Korean]] Peninsula and the mainland of the Russian Far East. Its waters are almost enclosed from the [[Pacific Ocean]] and, like the [[Mediterranean Sea]], it has almost no [[Tide|tides]]. Dissolved oxygen is elevated, giving high biological productivity and making fishing the dominant economic activity. Japan calls it the Sea of Japan, a name it says has been used internationally since the early 19th century. [[South Korea]] seeks to use East Sea alongside it, and [[North Korea]] prefers East Sea of Korea. In April 2026 the International Hydrographic Organization adopted a standard that replaces sea names with numerical identifiers.

Small inland sea entirely within [[Turkey]], separating the country's European and Asian sides. It links the [[Black Sea]] and the [[Aegean Sea]] through the [[Bosporus]] and [[Dardanelles]] straits, and is considered the smallest sea in the world. It covers 11,350 km² (4,380 sq mi), roughly 280 km by 80 km. The sea is named after Marmara Island, which is rich in [[Marble|marble]]. The North Anatolian Fault runs under the sea and has triggered several major earthquakes, including the August 1999 Marmara Earthquake, which was followed by a [[Tsunami|tsunami]] along its shores.
